name: Introduction to Data Science and AI
tag: Teach a computer to recognise patterns instead of giving it every answer.
goal: Spot patterns in shopping data, flowers, handwritten digits and messages.
road: W1 to 2: Collect data; turn images and words into numbers.
W3 to 4: Discover supervised, unsupervised and sequential learning; group similar items.
W5 to 6: Try nearest neighbours, decision trees and neural networks; classify images.
W7 to 8: See how feedback helps AI improve in questions, healthcare and robots.
task: Make a mini “sort the mystery objects” game: choose three features, then group objects by similarity.
friction: If “feature engineering” sounds scary, read it as choosing clues that matter.
verdict: Strong if curious about AI; some new vocabulary.
world: AI that identifies animals in camera photos, music recommendations, and systems that flag suspicious transactions.
scene: Try spotting what makes two images similar. That is the beginning of teaching a computer to recognise patterns.

name: Introduction to Electronic Systems
tag: Find out what is happening inside the phone and charger you use every day.
goal: Understand batteries, voltage, electrical signals, motors and power use.
road: W1 to 2: Peek inside a phone and read battery/charger labels.
W3 to 4: Learn voltage, current, resistance and power.
W5 to 6: Explore motors, microphones, generators and changing signals.
W7 to 8: Understand signal energy, harmonics and electricity bills.
task: Compare the wattage and voltage printed on two chargers (no opening or electrical experiments).
friction: The maths of waves and signals may feel unfamiliar; begin with phone components.
verdict: A practical topic, but circuit maths is a possible sticking point.
world: Noise-cancelling headphones, electric cars, wearable heart-rate sensors, and tiny satellites all rely on electronics.
scene: Your phone is not magic. It is an orchestra of circuits, sensors, and signals.

name: Introduction to Architecture and Design
tag: Redesign spaces that annoy you—and learn why some rooms just feel right.
goal: Play with shapes, colour, proportion, patterns and drawings of spaces.
road: W1 to 2: Notice architecture; build shapes from points and lines.
W3 to 4: Explore balance, scale and tangram compositions.
W5 to 6: Study rhythm and patterns; sketch plans, elevations and perspectives.
W7 to 8: Design logos and jaali patterns; pull a final design together.
task: Sketch your dream study corner with one change that makes it easier to use.
friction: No need to be “good at art” already; rough sketches count as thinking.
verdict: Great for visual, creative learners.
world: Architects create earthquake-aware buildings, shaded public spaces, and small homes that feel twice their size.
scene: What would you change about your classroom if you were the architect?

name: Introduction to Engineering Biological Systems
tag: What if living cells could help make medicine or useful materials?
goal: Meet cells, microscopes, proteins, DNA and the idea of engineering biology.
road: W1 to 2: Cells, microscopes and virtual biotech-lab tools.
W3 to 4: How biological products are made; membranes and carbohydrates.
W5 to 6: Proteins, enzymes, DNA and introductory bioinformatics.
W7 to 8: PCR, genetic engineering and biological production.
task: Draw a “cell factory” that turns ingredients into something useful; label its jobs.
friction: DNA amplification, PCR and BLAST are names of tools, not prerequisites.
verdict: Interesting if biology is already a favourite; technical words build up.
world: Engineered microbes can produce medicines such as insulin, and bioengineers build tissue models to study diseases.
scene: Imagine a tiny factory that is alive. What would you ask it to make?

name: Fun with Math and Computing
tag: How do computers search, keep secrets—and even count votes?
goal: Explore binary, fast searching, clever card tricks and cryptography.
road: W1 to 2: Binary and other ways computers represent numbers.
W3 to 4: Binary search, pattern matching and a 21-card trick.
W5 to 6: Fair voting and why election rules can be tricky.
W7 to 8: Codes, number theory and RSA-style security.
task: Play “guess my number” from 1 to 64 using yes/no questions; count how few guesses it takes.
friction: This is clever maths, not necessarily learning to code an app.
verdict: Best for puzzle-lovers; abstract concepts appear later.
world: Encryption helps protect private messages, and clever search algorithms find results without checking everything.
scene: Crack the trick: Why can seven yes-or-no questions identify a number from 1 to 100?

name: Math Unplugged: Games & Puzzles
tag: Chess puzzles, strange infinities and problems that still stump mathematicians.
goal: Think through chessboard tours, peg solitaire, infinities and playful proofs.
road: W1 to 2: Try knight tours across differently sized boards.
W3 to 4: Explore unusual chess moves and peg solitaire.
W5 to 6: Visit the impossible infinite hotel; compare infinities.
W7 to 8: Count areas with geometry; peek at unsolved problems.
task: Draw a 5×5 grid and see how far a chess knight can travel without repeating a square.
friction: Later lessons include graph theory and infinity ideas; getting stuck is normal.
verdict: Excellent if she likes puzzles more than textbook maths.
world: Puzzle ideas connect to delivery routes, network design, logic games, and mathematical research.
scene: Can you solve a board game by finding a clever pattern instead of trying every move?

name: The Fundamentals of Aerospace
tag: Why can planes fly, rockets launch, and satellites stay in orbit?
goal: Understand forces, airflow, engines, flight controls and space missions.
road: W1 to 2: Types of aircraft; forces and how air acts on objects.
W3 to 4: Wings, controls, speed and aircraft/rocket engines.
W5 to 6: Orbits, a Mars trip, parachutes and safe landing.
W7 to 8: Spinning wings and further flight applications.
task: Fold two paper plane designs and compare how far each flies in a safe open area.
friction: Words like drag and Mach number describe things you can first observe.
verdict: Very visual with strong real-world payoffs.
world: Engineers design reusable rockets, drones for difficult terrain, and spacecraft that navigate between planets.
scene: You can test an idea about flight with just a sheet of paper.

name: Humanities Unplugged
tag: Can a meme, song or ad change the way you see the world?
goal: Decode pop culture, identity, online influence and storytelling.
road: W1 to 2: Spot humanities in films and memes; decode cultural clues.
W3 to 4: Map your story; trace storytelling from ancient to digital.
W5 to 6: Analyse media bias, online identity and social change.
W7 to 8: Connect creative thinking with future directions.
task: Choose a favourite meme or ad: what emotion is it trying to trigger?
friction: This is about thinking critically, not memorising history dates.
verdict: Accessible if she likes stories, social media or film.
world: Film analysts decode visual storytelling, researchers study internet culture, and journalists investigate how narratives spread.
scene: A meme is a tiny cultural message. What is yours really saying?

name: Introduction to Ecology
tag: Become a detective for the plants, birds and tiny creatures around you.
goal: Track biodiversity using field observations, maps and real data.
road: W1 to 2: Observe biodiversity, species and local habitats.
W3 to 4: Create an iNaturalist-style observation project; compare regions.
W5 to 6: Explore biodiversity data and evolution.
W7 to 8: Study lizards, genes and the sounds of living things.
task: Photograph or sketch three different living things nearby, without disturbing them.
friction: Some data analysis uses spreadsheets; the outdoor observation comes first.
verdict: Strong for a curious observer who enjoys being outside.
world: Citizen scientists photograph species to help researchers map biodiversity and understand changes in habitats.
scene: The area outside your home can become your first research site.

name: Economics, Finance, and Money Matters
tag: Why do brands cost more, free things have catches, and prices rise?
goal: Explore money, inflation, risk, brands, trade and digital platforms.
road: W1 to 2: Money, value, inflation and brand-price comparisons.
W3 to 4: Incentives, risks and choices; probability exercises.
W5 to 6: Trade, market failures and game theory.
W7 to 8: Digital platforms and how technology changes markets.
task: Compare two similar products: what are you paying for besides the item?
friction: A little probability comes up, but most questions start in daily life.
verdict: Relatable for someone interested in shopping or decisions.
world: Economists study why prices change, how apps design incentives, and why people make surprising financial choices.
scene: Why do two nearly identical water bottles have wildly different prices?

name: Game Tech Explorers: Understanding Humans, Machines, and Play
tag: Imagine controlling a game with your voice, hands or body movement.
goal: Discover controllers, sensory feedback, game AI, gestures, voice and XR.
road: W1 to 2: Human senses, gaming sensors and rapid feedback.
W3 to 4: If to then game AI and gesture-based controls.
W5 to 6: Eye tracking, voice commands and immersive experiences.
W7 to 8: Try browser tools and create an interactive game feature.
task: Invent a character that reacts to three different voice commands or gestures.
friction: Some tools and sensor terms are new; the goal is a small feature, not a full game.
verdict: One of the most immediately engaging choices for a gamer.
world: Game studios use motion capture, voice controls, haptic feedback, and AI-powered characters.
scene: Design a controller that reacts when you wink, clap, or wave.

name: Introduction to Product Design
tag: Ever used something and thought: who designed this so badly?
goal: Learn to spot everyday problems and improve objects for real people.
road: W1 to 2: What designers do; identify annoying product problems.
W3 to 4: Understand users; compare shape, function and materials.
W5 to 6: Follow a design process and communicate ideas in sketches.
W7 to 8: Develop a simple design concept and explore careers.
task: Redesign a school-bag zipper, water bottle or pencil case; sketch your better version.
friction: The site says “senior secondary” in its description, but lists eligibility for IX–XII.
verdict: Good for creative problem-solvers; check the age-level mismatch.
world: Product designers improve easy-grip kitchen tools, accessible controllers, sports equipment, and everyday packaging.
scene: Find the most annoying object you use every day. That is your first design brief.

name: Molecular Engineering: Opportunities and Challenges
tag: Why can tiny molecules change colour, power screens or improve medicine?
goal: Explore how molecules are built and how they make useful materials.
road: W1 to 2: Simple/complex molecules and why things have colours.
W3: How scientists investigate reactions and interactions.
W4 to 6: Sensors, displays, medical imaging and solar energy.
W7 to 8: How to study chemistry and possible careers.
task: Pick one colourful object or LED and sketch questions about the materials inside it.
friction: Molecular interactions can feel abstract without a chemistry interest.
verdict: Better if she already enjoys chemistry.
world: Molecular engineering helps develop OLED displays, chemical sensors, battery materials, and advanced medical tools.
scene: The smallest building blocks can make the biggest difference in what a material does.

name: Introduction to Cybersecurity
tag: How do hackers trick people—and how can you protect your accounts?
goal: Passwords, secret codes, how the internet works and common attacks.
road: Module 1: What cybersecurity protects.
Module 2: Secrets and cryptography.
Module 3: Passwords and logging in securely.
Modules 4 to 5: Internet basics and popular cyberattacks.
task: Make a fake phishing-message checklist: identify suspicious links, urgency and strange senders.
friction: No hacking experience needed; the website describes about 10 hours of content.
verdict: High everyday relevance and clear short modules.
world: Security teams stop phishing attacks, protect accounts, and build systems that keep personal information private.
scene: Could you spot a fake login page before it steals a password?

name: Introduction to Digital Humanities
tag: What do games, AI, maps and stories reveal about people?
goal: Explore AI bias, immersive worlds, games, digital maps and portfolios.
road: M1 to 2: Digital humanities and bias in algorithms.
M3 to 4: AR/VR/XR and games as cultural stories.
M5 to 6: Learning games, mapping and digital storytelling.
M7 to 8: Build a digital portfolio; explore futures.
task: Map three places that matter to a fictional character and tell their story through them.
friction: Official page says no coding required and free browser tools.
verdict: Very accessible for someone who likes tech without programming.
world: Museums create interactive archives, researchers build historical maps, and artists explore AI and digital storytelling.
scene: What happens when you tell a story with a map instead of an essay?

name: Introduction to Forensic Sciences - I (For Classes IX & X)
tag: Fingerprint clues, suspicious messages and evidence that tells a story.
goal: Investigate prints, DNA, documents, digital evidence and crime scenes.
road: W1 to 2: Crime-scene clues and your fingerprints.
W3 to 4: Trace evidence, scene sketches and DNA investigation.
W5 to 6: Handwriting, language, manipulated digital evidence.
W7 to 8: Other evidence types and interpreting findings.
task: Create a fictional crime scene in a shoebox and draw an evidence map.
friction: The website says four expert-interview podcasts each week, hands-on work and Saturday live discussion—no conventional lectures.
verdict: Possibly the best match for a reluctant learner who likes mysteries.
world: Forensic teams compare fingerprints, study documents, analyse digital traces, and reconstruct what happened at a scene.
scene: A clue only helps if you can explain what it proves, and what it does not.

name: Introduction to Forensic Sciences - II (For Classes XI & XII)
tag: What does a real forensic scientist do all day?
goal: Meet forensic careers and learn pathways into lab, biology and other specialisms.
road: W1 to 2: Forensic job families and laboratory career routes.
W3 to 4: DNA lab and medicine-related pathways.
W5 to 6: Other professional pathways and evidence-based decisions.
W7 to 8: Career planning and defending an expert view.
task: Compare two forensic jobs: which daily tasks sound more interesting?
friction: NOT FOR GRADE 9: the official title restricts this one to Classes XI–XII.
verdict: Keep for later; choose Forensic Sciences I instead.
world: Forensic specialists work in labs, digital analysis, toxicology, and evidence interpretation.
scene: Do you prefer solving the science puzzle or presenting the evidence?

name: Our Defense System: How Our Body Detects and Defeats Invaders
tag: Your body has guards, rapid responders and specialists fighting invisible threats.
goal: Discover immunity, antibodies, vaccines, immune memory and what goes wrong.
road: Part 1: Body barriers and your fast-response immune team.
Part 2: Adaptive immunity and antibody specialists.
Part 3: Vaccines, memory and misfires.
Part 4: Colds, fever, discoveries and immunology careers.
task: Draw the immune system as a game team: shield, scout, fighter and memory keeper.
friction: “Innate” means ready-made defence; “adaptive” means a more targeted response.
verdict: Promising for someone who likes health or body science.
world: Immunologists help develop vaccines, study allergies, and investigate how the body recognises threats.
scene: Your body runs its own defence team, even while you are asleep.

name: From Statistics to Intelligence (For Classes XI & XII)
tag: Can averages mislead you? How do prediction apps guess what comes next?
goal: Study probability, surveys, misleading charts, prediction and AI.
road: W1 to 2: Chance and biased surveys.
W3 to 4: Averages, variation and big data patterns.
W5 to 6: Conditional probability, correlations and predictions.
W7 to 8: Data science, AI and possible careers.
task: Find two charts about the same topic and notice how their scales change the story.
friction: NOT FOR GRADE 9: explicitly intended for XI–XII, with advanced statistics.
verdict: Save for later; try Data Science and AI instead.
world: Statisticians help forecast demand, spot misleading surveys, and check whether a medical study is convincing.
scene: Can one chart tell a lie without containing a single false number?

name: Discover Engineering
tag: Find one thing that bothers people—and engineer a better version.
goal: Explore how engineers solve problems with science, creativity and teamwork.
road: W1 to 2: Find engineering in everyday objects and the science inside.
W3 to 4: Big engineering achievements and human needs.
W5 to 6: How engineers work; choose a problem worth solving.
W7 to 8: Develop an idea and present a short video pitch.
task: Find an annoying everyday object; explain the problem in 30 seconds before suggesting a fix.
friction: The goal is not to know all physics—start by noticing a problem.
verdict: Broad, practical and friendly for beginners.
world: Engineers create clean-water systems, safer roads, assistive technology, and solutions to everyday problems.
scene: Engineering begins with the sentence: This could work better.
